examples.title: Leaking kitchen faucet base
examples.input: My kitchen faucet is leaking from the base whenever I turn it on. House is ~1998, single-handle Moen pull-down, standard copper supply lines. I'm fairly handy and own a basic tool kit.
examples.output:
### Safety Check
No hazard. Turn off both under-sink shutoff valves and open the faucet to relieve pressure before starting.

### Diagnosis
Base leak on a single-handle pull-down almost always = worn cartridge O-rings/seals, not the supply lines. 1998-era Moen likely uses a 1225 cartridge family.

### Step-by-Step Method (reproducible)
1. Shut off supply valves, open faucet to drain. 2. Pop decorative cap, remove handle screw (2.5mm hex). 3. Remove handle, retaining clip, and dome. 4. Pull cartridge with Moen cartridge puller. 5. Replace O-rings + cartridge. 6. Reassemble; verify.

### Materials & Budget
Moen 1225 cartridge (~$18), O-ring kit (~$6), plumber's grease (~$5), cartridge puller (~$12). Total ~$41. Have: adjustable wrench, hex keys.

### Timeline & Permits
60–90 min, one phase. No permit required for in-kind faucet repair.

### Recommendation: DIY vs Pro
DIY. Low risk, low cost, matched to your skill level. A plumber would charge $150–$250 for the same fix. Hire a pro only if the cartridge is seized or the valve body is corroded.

### Verification & When to Escalate
Run hot/cold for 2 min, inspect base dry. Escalate if leak persists after cartridge swap (indicates cracked valve body = replace faucet).

examples.title: Flickering lights on one circuit
examples.input: Lights in my living room flicker, sometimes the whole circuit. Older home, maybe 1960s wiring, aluminum branch wiring I think. Not very experienced electrically.
examples.output:
### Safety Check
⚠️ STOP-AND-CALL-PRO. 1960s aluminum branch wiring + flickering across a whole circuit is a known fire-risk pattern (overheated connections). Do not open outlets or the panel yourself.

### Diagnosis
Likely loose/oxidized aluminum connections at devices or the breaker — a code and fire-safety issue, not a bulb problem.

### Step-by-Step Method
Reference-only (for understanding, not DIY): a licensed electrician inspects terminations, installs COPALUM crimps or AlumiConn connectors, and torque-checks the panel.

### Materials & Budget
Professional assessment $150–$300; remediation $150–$500+ per affected area. Full rewire if widespread: $8k–$15k.

### Timeline & Permits
Permit + inspection required for electrical work in most jurisdictions. 1–3 days depending on scope.

### Recommendation: DIY vs Pro
Hire a Pro — non-negotiable. Risk (fire), code, and permit requirements all point away from DIY regardless of skill. DIY would void insurance and endanger the home.

### Verification & When to Escalate
Confirm electrician provides a signed permit/inspection pass. Escalate immediately (shut off the breaker) if you smell burning or outlets feel warm before the visit.

tests.name: Routes safe low-risk task to DIY with full blueprint
tests.input: Running toilet, water keeps trickling into the bowl. Standard 2-piece toilet, flapper looks old. I'm comfortable with basic fixes.
tests.expected: No safety banner; diagnosis points to worn flapper/fill valve; reproducible steps with filled-in parts (flapper size, fill valve model), a small budget (~$15–$30), ~30 min timeline, no permit, and a DIY recommendation with verification checks for a dry overnight bowl.

tests.name: Escalates hazardous problem to professional before any DIY steps
tests.input: I smell gas near my furnace and the pilot keeps going out.
tests.expected: Output begins with a STOP-AND-CALL-PRO safety banner advising to leave the home and call the gas utility/emergency line; DIY steps are suppressed or marked reference-only; recommendation is Hire a Pro, citing life-safety risk and code.
